extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated electric utilities and EGUs, environmental lawyers, policy analysts, and notice-and-comment participants on CAA section 111 rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains statutory and interpretive criteria the EPA uses under Clean Air Act (CAA) section 111 to list source categories, determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER), set New Source Performance Standards (NSPS), and promulgate emission guidelines and state plans for existing Electric Utility Generating Units (EGUs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing source categories under CAA section 111(b)(1)(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(b)(1)(A) requires the EPA Administrator to promulgate a list of categories of stationary sources that the Administrator, in his or her judgment, finds “causes, or contributes significantly to, air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has authority to define the scope of the source categories, determine the pollutants for which standards should be developed, and distinguish among classes, types, and sizes within categories in establishing the standards. (Preamble discussion and citation of 40 CFR part 60 listings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of performance for new sources (NSPS) under CAA section 111(b)(1)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the EPA lists a source category, CAA section 111(b)(1)(B) requires the EPA to establish “standards of performance” for “new sources” in the source category. These standards are referred to as new source performance standards (NSPS) and are national requirements that apply directly to the sources subject to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAA section 111(a)(1) defines a “standard of performance” as “a standard for emissions of air pollutants” that is determined in a specified manner; CAA section 111(b)(1)(B) provides that standards of performance or revisions thereof shall become effective upon promulgation. NSPS must reflect the degree of emission limitation achievable through application of the BSER. (Preamble citations and statutory text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of “new source,” “stationary source,” “modification,” and “reconstruction”
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(2) defines a “new source”; 111(a)(3) defines “stationary source” as “any building, structure, facility, or installation which emits or may emit any air pollutant”; 111(a)(4) defines “modification” as any physical change or change in method of operation that increases emissions or results in emissions of a pollutant not previously emitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA regulations also treat a source that undergoes “reconstruction” as a new source. Under 40 CFR 60.15, “reconstruction” means replacement of components such that (1) the fixed capital cost of new components exceeds 50 percent of the fixed capital cost required to construct a comparable entirely new facility; and (2) it is technologically and economically feasible to meet the applicable standards. (Used to determine whether to treat projects as new-source subject to NSPS.)

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination framework under CAA section 111(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(1) requires that performance standards reflect “the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any non-air quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must first identify the “system[s] of emission reduction” that are “adequately demonstrated,” then determine the “best” of those systems taking into account factors including cost, non-air quality health and environmental impacts, and energy requirements. EPA then derives an “achievable” degree of emission limitation from that BSER. (Preamble discussion; West Virginia v. EPA cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of existing sources under CAA section 111(d) and state plans
rubrics_metrics.description: When the EPA establishes a standard for emissions from new sources, it must also, under CAA section 111(d), regulate emissions of that pollutant from existing sources in the same category, unless the pollutant is regulated under NAAQS (sections 108–110) or NESHAP (section 112). CAA 111(d) requires the Administrator to prescribe regulations that require each state to submit a plan establishing standards of performance for existing sources and providing for implementation and enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA promulgates “emission guidelines” that identify the BSER and the degree of emission limitation achievable through the BSER; each state must establish standards of performance for its sources that reflect that level of stringency. States need not compel regulated sources to adopt the particular components of the BSER, and states may include trading or averaging programs in their plans for compliance. Once EPA approves a state plan, its provisions become federally enforceable (like SIP provisions). If a state fails to submit a plan or submits an unsatisfactory plan, EPA must promulgate a federal plan. States may, in applying a standard to a particular source, consider factors including the remaining useful life of the source (42 U.S.C. 7411(d)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of EPA to review and revise NSPS (8-year review)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(b)(1)(B) requires EPA to “at least every 8 years, review and, if appropriate, revise” new source performance standards, though the Administrator need not review a standard if the Administrator determines review is not appropriate in light of readily available information on the efficacy of the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting an NSPS review, EPA has discretion to add emission limits for pollutants or emission sources not currently regulated for that source category. While CAA does not by its terms require EPA to review emission guidelines for existing sources, EPA retains authority to do so. (Preamble cites statutory text and prior Federal Register explanations, e.g., 81 FR 59277.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Thresholds for applying NSPS to modifications (large vs small)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2015 NSPS applied standards of performance to units undergoing “reconstruction” and to units undergoing “large modifications,” defined in that rule as modifications resulting in an increase in hourly CO2 emissions of more than 10 percent; it did not establish standards for “small modifications” (≤10% hourly CO2 increase) due to limited information to inform BSER analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates EPA's use of quantitative thresholds (e.g., >10% hourly CO2 increase) to decide whether a modification triggers NSPS coverage, and the role of available technical information in setting those thresholds. (2015 NSPS description in preamble.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of BSER determinations for new fossil fuel-fired steam generating units (2015 NSPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 2015 NSPS the EPA determined the BSER for newly constructed fossil fuel-fired steam generating units to be a new, highly efficient supercritical pulverized coal (SCPC) EGU that implements post-combustion partial CCS technology; EPA also identified natural gas co-firing and IGCC (with gas co-firing or partial CCS) as alternative methods of compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2015 NSPS reasoning included that CCS was adequately demonstrated, technically feasible, widely available, and implementable at reasonable cost. These are concrete exemplars of how EPA identifies and justifies particular technologies as BSER for a source category. (2015 NSPS summary in preamble.)

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER examples and approach for stationary combustion turbines (2015 NSPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: For newly constructed and reconstructed base load natural gas-fired stationary combustion turbines, the 2015 NSPS finalized a standard based on efficient NGCC technology as the BSER. For newly constructed and reconstructed non-base load natural gas-fired turbines and multi-fuel turbines, EPA finalized a heat input-based standard based on the use of lower-emitting fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA tailored BSER to source type and operating profile (base load vs non-base load) and used fuel-based metrics where appropriate. EPA declined to promulgate final standards for modified stationary combustion turbines due to lack of information. (2015 NSPS description in preamble.)

rubrics_metrics.name: CPP BSER for existing sources included generation-shifting measures
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Clean Power Plan (CPP), EPA identified three types of measures as the BSER for existing fossil fuel-fired steam EGUs: (1) improving heat rate at coal-fired steam plants; (2) substituting increased generation from lower-emitting NGCC plants for higher-emitting steam plants; and (3) substituting increased generation from new renewable energy sources for fossil steam plants. The latter two are characterized as “generation shifting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA based this BSER determination on a technical record evaluating generation shifting and on a legal interpretation that the term “system” in 111(a)(1) could encompass shifting generation from higher- to lower-emitting sources. EPA expressed that a state would have to ensure that the emissions standards it establishes (individually, in aggregate, or combined with other measures) represent the equivalent of performance rates derived from that BSER; states were not required to apply the specific measures identified and could include trading/averaging. (CPP summary in preamble.)

rubrics_metrics.name: ACE Rule interpretation limiting BSER to on-site/source-applied measures
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ACE Rule EPA interpreted the statutory term “system of emission reduction” to be limited to measures that can be applied to and at the level of the individual source (i.e., control measures that could be applied at each source), concluding that generation shifting is not such a control measure. Based on that legal interpretation, EPA found the BSER to be heat rate improvements alone for existing coal-fired steam-generating EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACE Rule rationale relied on the statutory text (e.g., that states must establish standards “for” “any existing source”) and on a major-rule presumption against reading BSER to encompass generation-shifting absent clear congressional statement. EPA listed various heat-rate-improvement technologies and provided ranges of expected reductions associated with those technologies. (ACE Rule summary in preamble.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial history as a constraint on EPA's interpretations and determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Key court decisions — Massachusetts v. EPA, AEP v. Connecticut, American Lung Ass'n v. EPA, and West Virginia v. EPA — shape the boundaries of EPA authority under CAA section 111. The D.C. Circuit confirmed EPA's authority to promulgate requirements under section 111 for GHGs from fossil fuel-fired EGUs notwithstanding section 112 regulation; West Virginia constrained aspects of how EPA may interpret BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites that American Lung Ass'n upheld EPA's alternative findings in the 2015 NSPS and that West Virginia is invoked in framing the BSER analysis. The preamble notes EPA is not reopening certain determinations from the 2015 NSPS and explains how prior litigation affects both past and present rulemaking choices. (Preamble legal-history discussion.)
